---
title: "Relative extremes: percentiles and spells"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A fixed threshold, such as 30 C, means different things in different places.
A relative threshold compares each day with what is usual for that place and
that time of year: a day is extreme when it is above the 95th percentile of
the same calendar month at the same location. This article computes such
indicators for precipitation.

```{r setup}
library(c4e)

survey <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "survey.csv", package = "c4e"))
survey$interview <- as.Date(survey$interview)
coord <- prepare_coord(survey, lat_var = lat, lon_var = lon,
                       id = hhid, interview = interview)

pre <- read_climate(system.file("extdata", "pre_daily.tif", package = "c4e"))
extracted <- extract_by_coord(pre, georef_coord(coord))
```

## Percentiles by location and month

`calc_percentile()` computes, for each location and calendar month, the
percentiles of the daily values. For precipitation, dry days would pull the
percentiles to zero, so days below 0.1 mm are left out: the percentiles
describe wet days. A `baseline` restricts the dates used, so a reference
period can be kept apart from the period studied.

```{r percentiles}
pct <- calc_percentile(extracted, p = c(0.9, 0.95), exclude_below = 0.1,
                       baseline = c("2021-01-01", "2022-12-31"))
head(pct, 4)
```

The result is a lookup table: one row per location and month. It records
which percentile each column holds and which days it was computed on.

## Days beyond the percentiles

`calc_percentile_day()` compares each day with its location's percentile
for that month. The direction follows the percentile: above for high ones,
below for low ones.

```{r rel-days}
days <- calc_percentile_day(extracted, pct)
dplyr::filter(days, day_abv_95p) |> head(3)
```

`mm_abv_95p` is how far above the percentile each day is, in millimetres:
the excess rainfall.

## Spells and their length

Spells of days above the percentile work as for fixed thresholds.
`calc_spell_percentile()` then asks how long a spell usually is, by location
and month, and `calc_spell_excess()` counts the days by which each spell
goes beyond that usual length.

```{r spells}
spells <- calc_spell(days, min_spell = 2)
spell_pct <- calc_spell_percentile(spells, p = 0.9)
spell_excess <- calc_spell_excess(spells, spell_pct)
names(spell_excess)
```

## Before each interview

The window summaries treat every indicator by its kind: days are counted,
excesses summed, spells summarised.

```{r summary}
summary <- summarise_by_interview(coord, spell_excess, window = window_lag("1 year"))
print(summary, n = 4)
c4e_labels(summary)[c("day_abv_95p_sum", "mm_abv_95p_sum")]
```

## In one call

`weather_extremes()` does the same with a preset: `wet_days_p95` asks for
the 95th and 99th percentiles of wet days. Here the same call with
`p = 0.95` and the spell excess switched on:

```{r wrapper}
wet <- weather_extremes(survey, system.file("extdata", "pre_daily.tif", package = "c4e"),
                        id = hhid, interview = interview, p = 0.95,
                        control = extremes_control(spell_excess = TRUE, verbose = FALSE))
names(wet)
```
